purpose: Third deep-expansion pass covering the next eight adjacent records with populated historical, organizational, textual, geographic, relational and evidence layers.

identity.name: Ordo Templi Orientis
identity.geographic_core: German-speaking Europe, Britain, North America and later international branches

foundational_figures: Heinrich Tränker and other early collaborators
formation.historical_field: Masonic and Rosicrucian revival, Theosophy, European occultism and Lebensreform milieus
formation.masonic_context: The order developed from a confederation of Masonic-derived rites; its Masonic regularity and succession claims were contested.
formation.crowley_period: Aleister Crowley became increasingly central after his contact with Theodor Reuss and subsequently reorganized the order around Thelema.

worldview.framework: A syncretic esoteric system combining initiatory symbolism, Thelema, Hermetic and Masonic forms and ritual magic.
worldview.thelemic_layer: Under Crowley, OTO became a principal organizational vehicle for Thelema.
worldview.initiation: Progress through degrees is intended to develop knowledge, discipline and participation in the order's esoteric system.

practice.initiation: The order uses graded initiation and lodge-based instruction.
practice.gnostic_mass: Ecclesia Gnostica Catholica's Gnostic Mass became a major public-facing ritual expression of Thelemic OTO practice.
practice.study: Members encounter ritual, symbolic, philosophical and magical instruction appropriate to organizational degree.
practice.integrity: Detailed sexual-magic material is historically relevant but is recorded here descriptively rather than as operational instruction.

texts.textual_status: The corpus is organizational and initiatory rather than a single closed scripture.

people.succession: Leadership after Reuss and Crowley generated competing claims and later organizational lineages.

organization.structure: Graded initiatory order with local lodges, camps and affiliated bodies.
organization.degrees: The order inherited and modified a multi-degree Masonic-style architecture.
organization.governance: Supreme leadership claims changed over time; post-Crowley succession is historically complex.
organization.internationality: Branches developed in Europe and North America and later in other countries.

geography.evidence: Charters, correspondence, membership records and lodge histories provide the strongest organizational evidence.

society.culture: OTO contributed to the twentieth-century Western occult and alternative-religion milieu.
society.public_private: Much work is initiatory and private, while selected rituals and publications are public.
society.reception: It became one of the best-known institutional carriers of Crowleyan Thelema.

evidence.confidence: high for organizational history, major figures, documents and Thelemic reorganization; lower for disputed early lineage and succession claims

sources.title: The Unknown God: W. T. Smith and the Thelemites

contested: Masonic legitimacy of early OTO claims
exact chronology of some early reorganizations

identity.name: Theosophical Society
identity.geographic_core: New York, India and international lodge networks

formation.foundation: Organized in New York in 1875; November 17, 1875 is conventionally treated by the Society as the formal founding date.
formation.historical_field: Spiritualism, Western esotericism, comparative religion, Orientalist scholarship and occult revival.
formation.india_transition: Blavatsky and Olcott moved to India in 1878–79; international headquarters were established at Adyar in 1882.
formation.institutional_split: The movement later developed multiple organizational branches, including Adyar and American and other national organizations.

core_aims: comparative study of religion, philosophy and science
investigation of unexplained laws of nature and latent human capacities
worldview.cosmology: Modern Theosophy developed a complex evolutionary cosmology involving cycles, planes, reincarnation and spiritual development.
worldview.masters: Blavatsky and the movement described advanced adepts or Masters; their existence is a religious/esoteric claim rather than established empirical fact.
worldview.human_development: Humanity is presented as participating in a long spiritual evolution toward expanded consciousness.

practice.study: Comparative reading, lectures, meditation and esoteric study became important forms of participation.
practice.lodge_life: Local lodges and study centers formed the basic organizational units.
practice.service: Olcott and other leaders connected Theosophical activity with educational and Buddhist revival work in South Asia.
practice.esoteric_work: Selected members pursued more specialized esoteric study through inner or esoteric sections.

texts.institutional: Theosophical journals, correspondence, constitutions and lecture literature are major historical sources.
texts.textual_limit: The writings combine comparative scholarship, religious teaching, claimed revelation and speculative cosmology; these layers must remain distinct.

people.steiner_relation: Steiner became general secretary of the German section before breaking with the Society and developing Anthroposophy.

organization.structure: International association with national sections, local lodges and changing esoteric structures.
organization.headquarters: Adyar became the international headquarters in 1882.
organization.branches: Major organizational divisions emerged over leadership, doctrine and institutional authority.

geography.global_reach: The Society established lodges across Europe, Asia, the Americas and elsewhere.

society.religion_comparison: The Society promoted comparative study and deliberately crossed boundaries between Western and Asian religious concepts.
society.south_asia: Olcott's Buddhist educational and revival activities are an important part of the Society's historical footprint.
society.modernism: Theosophy influenced literature, art, modernist spirituality and later occult organizations.

evidence.confidence: high for organizational history, publications and institutional movement; lower for supernatural and hidden-Master claims

sources.title: Brief History of the Theosophical Society

evidence.integrity: Community self-description and historical reconstruction are maintained as separate evidence layers.

identity.name: Anthroposophy
identity.geographic_core: Central Europe, Switzerland and later global networks

formation.precursor: Steiner emerged from the German-speaking Theosophical milieu and became general secretary of the German Section before breaking with the Theosophical Society.
formation.formation: Anthroposophy developed as Steiner's distinct spiritual-scientific movement in the early twentieth century.
formation.institutionalization: The Anthroposophical Society and later the Goetheanum became principal institutional centers.

worldview.core: Anthroposophy presents spiritual knowledge as a disciplined path of investigation into human beings, nature and cosmic evolution.
worldview.human_model: Steiner describes human development through physical, soul and spiritual dimensions and successive stages of consciousness.
worldview.christology: Christ occupies a central role in Steiner's esoteric interpretation of human and cosmic evolution.
worldview.reincarnation: Reincarnation and karma are major components of the worldview.

practice.meditation: Meditative concentration and exercises for developing attention and spiritual perception are central.
practice.education: Waldorf education applies selected anthroposophical developmental ideas in educational practice.
practice.agriculture: Steiner's 1924 Agriculture Course became the basis of biodynamic agriculture.
practice.arts: Eurythmy, architecture, visual arts and speech work developed as anthroposophically influenced practices.

texts.status: Steiner's books and thousands of lectures constitute the principal textual corpus.
texts.interpretation: The texts mix philosophical argument, esoteric revelation, spiritual biography and practical institutional guidance.

people.legacy: Later practitioners developed anthroposophical initiatives in education, agriculture, medicine, arts and social organization.

organization.school_network: Waldorf schools form a major global institutional network influenced by Steiner's educational work.
organization.governance: The Society has national and regional structures connected to the Goetheanum.

geography.global: Anthroposophical schools and initiatives developed across Europe, North America, Latin America, Africa, Asia and Oceania.

society.environment: Anthroposophy has influenced environmental and agricultural movements, especially through biodynamics.
society.education: Waldorf education is its most internationally visible institutional application.
society.medicine: Anthroposophically oriented medicine exists as a distinct historical and institutional current; its empirical claims require separate evaluation from its spiritual framework.

evidence.confidence: high for Steiner's biography, organizations, publications and institutional history; theological and scientific claims require separate evidentiary treatment

sources.title: Eco-Alchemy: Anthroposophy and the History and Future of Environmentalism

evidence.integrity: Institutional history is not treated as validation of anthroposophical supernatural or medical claims.

identity.name: Church of Satan
identity.geographic_core: United States, especially San Francisco at formation

formation.foundation: LaVey publicly established the Church of Satan in San Francisco in 1966.
formation.historical_field: 1960s counterculture, secularization, Western occult revival and literary Satanic symbolism.
precursors: Process Church milieu as a later comparison rather than a direct organizational predecessor
formation.codification: The Satanic Bible, published in 1969, became the movement's best-known textual statement.

worldview.theology: The Church's LaVeyan form is generally described as non-theistic or atheistic Satanism.
worldview.satan_symbol: Satan functions primarily as a symbol of individualism, self-assertion, natural desire and opposition to conventional religious morality.
worldview.ethics: Personal responsibility, self-preservation and individual liberty are emphasized, with ritual used partly as psychodramatic expression.
worldview.anti_religion: Its critique targets conventional Christian morality and what LaVey regarded as repressive religious norms.

practice.ritual: Ritual is framed largely as psychodrama and symbolic magic rather than worship of a literal Satan.
practice.celebration: Individual and group ceremonial practice exists alongside secular everyday life.
practice.initiation: The organization has used degrees, titles and formal membership structures, though participation and institutional arrangements have changed over time.

texts.interpretive_note: The texts are primary sources for LaVeyan self-description but do not establish claims about ancient Satan worship.

people.important_successors: The organization continued under later administrators after LaVey's death, while other Satanic organizations developed independently.

organization.form: Religious organization with formal clergy/titular structure and local or affiliated activity.
organization.schism: Michael Aquino and others departed in 1975 and formed the Temple of Set.
organization.institutional_identity: The Church of Satan remains distinct from later organizations such as The Satanic Temple.

geography.expansion: The organization and its literature reached a national and international audience through books, media and correspondence.

society.counterculture: The Church became a prominent symbol of 1960s and 1970s countercultural religion.
society.media: Media attention played a major role in constructing public perceptions of LaVey and Satanism.
society.moral_panic: Later Satanic Panic narratives should be separated from documented Church practices and organizational history.

evidence.confidence: high for founding, publications and organizational history; interpretation of doctrine should use LaVeyan texts and scholarly analysis

sources.title: Children of Lucifer: The Origins of Modern Religious Satanism
The Age of Satanism: Anton LaVey and the Church of Satan

evidence.integrity: Self-identification, scholarly classification and hostile accusations remain separate fields.

formation.emergence: The Satanic Temple emerged in the early 2010s in the United States and developed rapidly through public campaigns and media activity.
formation.historical_field: Secularism, religious pluralism, church-state law, internet culture and modern Satanic identity.
formation.distinction: It is organizationally and doctrinally distinct from the Church of Satan.

worldview.theology: The movement generally presents Satan symbolically rather than as a literal supernatural being.
worldview.ethical_framework: Its Seven Fundamental Tenets emphasize compassion, reason, bodily autonomy, personal freedom and proportional justice.
worldview.satan_symbol: Satan is presented as a symbol of rebellion against arbitrary authority and defense of individual autonomy.
worldview.politics: The organization does not identify simply with one political party, although its campaigns often intersect with progressive or civil-liberties causes.

practice.rituals: Members may use ceremonies and rituals as meaningful religious or symbolic expression.
practice.activism: Public campaigns concerning religious equality, reproductive rights, bodily autonomy and church-state separation are central to its identity.
practice.community: Chapters and online networks provide community structures.

texts.comparative: The 2017 Greaves text explicitly contrasts TST with the Church of Satan and is useful as a self-representational primary source.

organization.form: Contemporary religious organization with chapters, membership structures and central public advocacy.
organization.public_strategy: Legal and media campaigns are used to test the practical meaning of religious pluralism.
organization.identity_boundary: TST rejects identification with the Church of Satan despite shared Satanic terminology.

geography.reach: International online and organizational presence has developed around local chapters and campaigns.

society.law: Religious-liberty litigation and public-policy disputes are important to its public activity.
society.media: Internet campaigns and viral publicity are central to recruitment and public visibility.
society.pluralism: Its existence provides a contemporary case study in how minority religions use equal-treatment principles in secular states.

relationships.shared_symbol: Satanic symbolism is shared with other modern Satanisms but interpreted differently.

evidence.confidence: high for public organizational activity, texts and campaigns; internal membership demographics require cautious sourcing

sources.title: Lucien Greaves (The Satanic Temple), 'Church of Satan vs. Satanic Temple'

evidence.integrity: Record self-description separately from external political characterization.

identity.name: Temple of Set
identity.geographic_core: United States with international initiatory network

formation.origin: The Temple of Set formed in 1975 following Aquino's break with the Church of Satan.
formation.historical_field: Post-LaVeyan Satanism, Western esotericism and Egyptian religious symbolism.
formation.doctrinal_shift: Aquino rejected the Church of Satan's symbolic interpretation of Satan and developed a Set-centered theology.

worldview.central_principle: Set is understood as a metaphysical and initiatory principle associated with individual consciousness and self-becoming.
worldview.xeper: Xeper, commonly translated in the movement as becoming or self-becoming, is a central initiatory concept.
worldview.individuality: The tradition emphasizes development of the individual self rather than submission to a conventional creator deity.
worldview.egyptian_connection: The movement invokes the ancient Egyptian god Set, but modern Setian theology is not treated as an unchanged continuation of ancient Egyptian religion.

practice.initiation: Initiatory work proceeds through degrees and individual study.
practice.magic: Ritual and magical practices are framed as means of transformation and consciousness development.
practice.study: Members work with Setian texts, symbols and philosophical exercises.
practice.pylons: Pylons function as organizational and initiatory groupings within the movement.

central: The Book of Coming Forth by Night
Temple of Set writings and degree material
texts.foundational_text: Aquino's 1975 text presents itself as a revelation associated with Set.
texts.interpretive_limit: The text is primary evidence for Setian self-understanding, not independent proof of supernatural revelation.

people.early_context: Other former Church of Satan members participated in the movement's formation.

organization.structure: Priesthood, Council of Nine, pylons and graded initiatory degrees.
organization.membership: The organization emphasizes selective initiatory participation rather than mass public membership.
organization.authority: Priestly and initiatory status provides organizational authority.

geography.network: International membership developed through local and correspondence-based initiatory structures.

society.classification: Scholars variously place it within Satanism, post-Satanism or the Left-Hand Path.
society.reception: It is an important case for studying how modern religious movements reinterpret ancient deities without claiming simple historical continuity.
society.media: Public understanding has often been shaped by sensational accounts rather than internal documents.

evidence.confidence: high for 1975 formation, Aquino's role and surviving texts; moderate for internal organizational history outside public records

sources.title: Michael Aquino, The Book of Coming Forth by Night (1975)
Satanism: A Reader, chapter on Michael Aquino

evidence.integrity: Ancient Egyptian Set and modern Setian religion are linked by symbolic reference, not assumed institutional continuity.

identity.name: Order of Nine Angles
identity.geographic_core: United Kingdom and transnational online networks
identity.attributed_founder: The movement is associated with the pseudonym Anton Long; authorship and organizational origins are contested.

formation.historical_field: British occult milieu, Satanism, National Socialist and radical political esotericism.
formation.origin_claims: ONA texts claim ancient or traditional origins, but these lineage claims are not accepted as independently established historical fact.
formation.development: The movement circulated through texts, small cells and later online dissemination rather than a transparent centralized institution.

worldview.framework: The 'Sinister Tradition' combines occult self-transformation with radical transgression and political-esoteric themes.
worldview.transgression: Transgression is framed in ONA literature as a method of developing individuals and challenging conventional moral boundaries.
worldview.political_overlap: Academic research documents intersections with National Socialist and radical Islamist milieus in the work of figures associated with the movement.
worldview.integrity: These political and extremist dimensions are documented as historical subject matter, not endorsed.

practice.structure: Texts describe initiatory stages and ordeals, but the archive should not reproduce operational instructions for extremist or harmful activity.
practice.texts: The movement relies heavily on internally circulated manuals and mythic-historical narratives.
practice.risk_layer: Operationally harmful, criminal or extremist instructions are intentionally summarized rather than reproduced.

texts.black_book: The Black Book of Satan is treated by scholarship as an important early textual expression of the movement.
texts.textual_status: Texts are primary evidence for self-description but do not prove claimed ancient lineage.

people.authorship_problem: Pseudonymous authorship and shifting identities make biographical attribution uncertain in parts of the corpus.

organization.form: Loose occult network with cells, pseudonymous authorship and decentralized textual dissemination.
organization.centralization: No transparent conventional hierarchy comparable to a public church is established.
organization.security: Its deliberately opaque structure complicates membership and organizational estimates.

geography.later_reach: International online circulation and ideological influence extend beyond the United Kingdom.

society.extremism: ONA is significant to research on the intersection of occultism and extremist politics.
society.terrorism_relevance: Academic research has documented links between associated figures and violent extremist milieus; these links should be separately attributed rather than generalized to every person encountering ONA texts.
society.media: Internet dissemination has expanded access to ONA material and blurred organizational boundaries.

documented_intersections: David Myatt's extremist writings and activities

evidence.confidence: high for existence of ONA texts and its ideological corpus; moderate for early organizational history; lower for pseudonymous origin claims

sources.title: The Order of the Nine Angles, The Black Book of Satan (1984)
Secret Identities in the Sinister Tradition

evidence.integrity: No romanticization, recruitment or operationalization; distinguish texts, ideology, attributed individuals and independently documented actions.

identity.name: Process Church of the Final Judgment
identity.category: new religious movement / apocalyptic esoteric religion
identity.geographic_core: United Kingdom and United States, especially California

formation.origin: The movement developed from a relationship between Robert and Mary Anne de Grimston and an earlier Scientology-linked background before becoming an independent religious movement.
formation.historical_field: 1960s counterculture, occult revival, Scientology-adjacent experimentation and apocalyptic Christianity/Satanism.
formation.expansion: The group established centers and communities in several locations, especially in the United States.

worldview.core_theology: The Process Church developed a distinctive theology in which apparently opposed divine figures could be understood as aspects of a larger cosmic unity.
worldview.apocalypse: Apocalyptic transformation and the reconciliation of opposites were important themes.
worldview.integrity: The group's theology should be reconstructed from its own publications rather than later conspiracy literature.

practice.community: Members participated in communal religious life and organized centers.
practice.worship: Ritual and devotional practices drew on Christian and Satanic imagery in the movement's own syncretic framework.
practice.publications: Magazines and pamphlets were major vehicles of doctrine and recruitment.
practice.animal_welfare: Later phases of the organization included animal-welfare activity under changed institutional forms.

texts.status: Published texts provide unusually direct evidence for theology and public self-presentation.
texts.scholarly_use: Oxford scholarship treats the group's texts as primary sources for its unusual synthesis of Christian and Satanic symbolism.

people.leadership: The de Grimstons were central to the movement's development and doctrinal direction.

organization.form: Communal religious movement with centers in several countries.
organization.membership: Participation involved community life and disciplined religious identity.
organization.transformation: The movement underwent significant organizational change during the 1970s rather than continuing unchanged.

major_centers: Los Angeles and other California locations
geography.expansion: The movement operated internationally for a limited period.

society.counterculture: The Process Church became associated with 1960s and 1970s counterculture and alternative religion.
society.conspiracy: Later conspiracy narratives frequently exaggerated or invented links to unrelated criminal events; these claims must not substitute for documentary evidence.
society.media: Its unusual theology and visual style attracted substantial media attention.

relationships.comparative: Its synthesis of Jehovah, Christ, Lucifer and Satan makes it especially useful for studying religious boundary-crossing.

evidence.confidence: high for existence, founders, publications and major theological themes; moderate for detailed internal membership history
strongest_sources: academic histories of Satanism and new religious movements

sources.title: The Process Church of the Final Judgement, 'The Gods on War' and 'The Gods and Their People'

evidence.integrity: Documented history is kept separate from later conspiracy narratives and criminal accusations.
